title: In 8 human autosomes, point mutations that make moderate transcription-factor motif matches in non-functional DNA show no more selection than shuffled-motif controls; lost existing matches show some
abstract: Point mutations that create new moderate transcription-factor (TF) motif matches in non-functional human DNA are not rarer, and not less often observed, in 76,215 genomes than mutations that create matches to shuffled motifs. This matters because random DNA has regulatory activity by default, so a large genome must either tolerate new spurious TF sites or keep its non-functional DNA quiet by selection. We used gnomAD v4.1 single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) on 8 complete autosomes (about 20% of the genome; 74 million observed SNVs and, in a 50% sample of positions, 599 million possible SNVs) in DNA that is more than 200 bp from ENCODE candidate regulatory elements, not conserved in mammals, and not in exons or repeats. A moderate gain creates a match to one of 26 JASPAR motifs at p < 1e-4; the null is the same motifs with shuffled columns. Two tests measure purifying selection: an excess of singletons (alleles seen once) and a depletion of possible SNVs that are never observed. Real minus shuffled moderate gains gave +0.04 percentage points (pp; 95% interval -0.23 to +0.30) in the singleton test and -0.018 pp (-0.078 to +0.043) in the depletion test, with no signal near genes or next to dosage-sensitive genes. For comparison, new cryptic splice sites in the same DNA gave a singleton excess of +2.99 pp, and mammal-conserved sites +0.83 pp and a depletion of -0.202 pp. In SuRE reporter data the motif calls shifted activity in the expected direction. Strong gains (p < 1e-6) were not resolved. Mutations that remove existing real motif matches showed selection in both tests (+0.20 pp, +0.05 to +0.35; -0.062 pp, -0.092 to -0.031; robust to Roulette mutation rates), but this signal is not significant per motif and is enriched in Alu copies. Main limitations: 8 of 22 autosomes, motif matches as a proxy for binding, a null whose spread limits precision, and tests that detect only selection of about 1e-3 or stronger.

display.caption: SNVs in non-functional human DNA (8 autosomes), observed minus expected under a 7-mer x region model fitted without motif-change SNVs (percentage points; selection to the right). Blue: real motifs (26-motif unions) with 95% block-bootstrap interval; orange: the 4 shuffled-motif unions; green: conserved-site reference and new cryptic splice sites (positive control). A: singleton excess. B: depletion of possible SNVs (expected minus observed).

Real minus shuffled motifs (percentage points, selection upwards) for level-1 gains and losses, by distance to the nearest protein-coding TSS, by s_het of that gene, and outside transposons. 95% intervals include the spread between the 4 shuffle sets.
SuRE reporter assay (K562, HepG2): change of activity (log2 ALT/REF minus all SNVs) for SNVs that gain or lose real motif matches (blue, 95% CI) and shuffled-motif matches (orange).

Constraint of validated enhancers depends on target-gene dosage sensitivity; we test whether selection on new TF sites depends on s_het in the same way.
